planting.note: Divide offsets or root leaf cuttings in spring; grow in bright shade with high humidity and freely draining, humus-rich mix, protecting from frost below about 40F.

directions: Streptocarpus rexii is the original South African species from which nearly all modern Cape primrose hybrids descend, forming a stemless rosette of long, velvety, strap-shaped leaves from wooded ravine and coastal-mountain habitat in the Eastern and Western Cape. In frost-free climates it can be grown outdoors in dappled shade; elsewhere it is a reliable houseplant on a bright windowsill out of direct sun, producing slender stalks of lilac-blue, trumpet-shaped flowers over a long season. Propagate readily from leaf-section cuttings laid on damp, sterile medium, and keep the thin roots evenly moist but never waterlogged. Avoid cold drafts and overwatering, both of which quickly cause leaf-tip dieback and crown rot.

planting.note: Start from fresh seed or offsets in spring in bright, humid shade; this unifoliate species dies back to its single giant leaf's base after flowering and resents cold, wet dormancy.

directions: Native to rocky grassland and forest-margin seepage sites of South Africa's former Transvaal goldfields, Streptocarpus dunnii is a striking unifoliate species that produces just one enormous, puckered, felted leaf lying flat against the ground before sending up a dense cluster of salmon-red to brick-red tubular flowers on short stalks. Grow in bright, filtered shade with constant humidity and a very free-draining, humus-rich substrate, since the single leaf is prone to rot if water sits on its surface. After flowering the plant typically goes into a resting phase; keep it on the dry side and barely above cool-temperate minimums until new growth resumes. It is a specialty item for gesneriad collectors rather than a mass-market houseplant.

planting.note: Grow in deep, warm shade with high humidity; the single enormous quilted leaf needs ample room and freely draining mix to avoid rot.

directions: Streptocarpus wendlandii, from forested ravines of South Africa's old Transvaal region, is grown chiefly as a novelty foliage plant: it produces a single, enormous, dark-green leaf with a silvery sheen and purple underside that can spread well over a foot across, with a cluster of small pale lavender flowers emerging from its base. It needs deep, warm shade, high humidity, and a coarse, well-aerated potting mix, since the flat leaf collects moisture and rots easily if misted or watered overhead. Give it a sheltered terrarium-like microclimate rather than open garden exposure, and propagate by seed or by rooting a leaf section, as offsets are rare. This is a collector's curiosity best suited to shaded greenhouse or terrarium culture.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in warm, humid shade in a light, fast-draining mix; unlike rosette-forming relatives, this species branches on true above-ground stems.

directions: Streptocarpus caulescens is one of the caulescent (stem-forming) Streptocarpus species from the montane forests of Kenya and Tanzania, trailing or scrambling on soft, fleshy stems rather than forming a flat rosette like most of its relatives. Small pale violet, tubular flowers appear in loose clusters along the stems through much of the warm season. It thrives in warm, humid, shaded conditions reminiscent of an East African cloud forest understory, making it well suited to a hanging basket in a shaded porch or greenhouse. Propagate easily from stem cuttings rooted in a light, moisture-retentive mix, and pinch growing tips periodically to keep the trailing stems bushy rather than leggy.

planting.note: Divide rosettes or root leaf cuttings in spring in bright, humid shade; keep humus-rich mix evenly moist but fast-draining.

directions: Native to forested ravines of South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, Streptocarpus candidus forms a low rosette of textured, hairy leaves and is notable among its relatives for its fragrant, pale flowers, which release a soft sweet scent most noticeable in the evening. Grow exactly as for its close relative Streptocarpus rexii: bright, indirect shade, high humidity, and a light, humus-rich, well-drained potting mix that never sits wet at the roots. It makes an interesting addition to a shaded windowsill collection of Cape primroses where scent, not just color, extends the plant's seasonal interest. Propagate from leaf cuttings or by division of offset rosettes.

planting.note: Start the tuber into growth in warm, humid, bright shade once nighttime temperatures stay above 60F; keep nearly dry and cool during its winter dormancy.

directions: Sinningia iarae is a Brazilian tuberous gesneriad prized among succulent and caudiciform collectors for its disproportionately large, partly exposed woody tuber, from which soft, hairy leaves and tubular red-orange flowers emerge each growing season. Grow in bright, filtered shade in a gritty, fast-draining mix, allowing the tuber's shoulder to sit at or just above the soil surface as it would on an exposed rocky outcrop in its native habitat. Water regularly through the warm growing season but withhold water almost entirely once the foliage dies back for its dry-season dormancy, storing the dormant tuber in a cool, dry spot. It is best grown as a container specimen for a bright, shaded windowsill or greenhouse bench rather than planted in open garden soil.

planting.note: Plant tubers after frost danger passes in a warm, humid, partly shaded spot; in zone 7 gardens the tuber can overwinter in the ground under a deep dry mulch.

directions: Sinningia tubiflora, native to grassland and scrub from Brazil to Argentina, is unusually cold-tolerant for a tuberous gesneriad and is grown outdoors as far north as USDA zone 7 with deep winter mulch over the dormant tuber. It spreads by underground rhizomes into loose colonies of upright, softly hairy stems, topped from midsummer into fall by clusters of large, powerfully sweet-scented, narrow white tubular flowers that attract hawkmoths at dusk. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright part shade, and let the clump die back naturally with the first hard frost, resuming growth from the tuber the following late spring. Its fragrance alone earns it a spot near a shaded patio or evening seating area.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plants Database

planting.note: Start tubers into growth in warm, bright shade once temperatures are reliably above 60F at night; keep dry and cool through winter dormancy.

directions: Sinningia warmingii is a Brazilian tuberous species grown by gesneriad enthusiasts for its showy pendant, tubular flowers that range from orange-red to pink depending on the form, held above a low clump of velvety leaves. As with most Brazilian Sinningia, it needs bright, filtered shade, high humidity during active growth, and a sharply draining mix over a season of dry winter dormancy once the foliage collapses. Grow it as a container plant where its dormant tuber can be kept dry and protected from frost, moving it to a brighter, more humid spot as new growth resumes in spring. It pairs well with other Gesneriaceae in a shaded collector's bench display.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil under deciduous shade; this rare Klamath-Siskiyou endemic is very slow from seed, so bulbs or divisions establish faster.

directions: Known only from a small area of the Klamath-Siskiyou Mountains straddling the California-Oregon border, Taylor's fawn lily grows on wooded, often serpentine slopes where it blooms in early spring with one or two nodding, deep rose-pink flowers above a pair of plain green, unmottled leaves. It should be planted in dappled shade under deciduous trees in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil that stays moist through its spring growth and dries out somewhat as it goes dormant in summer heat. Given its very restricted native range, source bulbs only from a reputable specialty bulb nursery propagating stock, never from wild populations.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil under light high-elevation forest shade; very slow to establish from seed.

directions: The Kaweah fawn lily is a rare California endemic restricted to a small area of the southern Sierra Nevada's Tulare County, growing on open to lightly wooded slopes near the Kaweah River drainage where it flowers in spring with creamy white to pale yellow, nodding blooms above mottled green leaves. In cultivation it wants the same cool, gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil and light high-elevation forest shade of its native range, with ample spring moisture and a dry summer dormancy. Because it is uncommon in the wild, grow only nursery-propagated bulbs from a specialty native-bulb source, siting them in a woodland-edge or rock garden bed that is not disturbed once the bulbs go dormant.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich soil under conifer shade, replicating the damp Olympic Peninsula forest floor; very slow from seed.

directions: The Olympic fawn lily is known only from a small number of sites on Washington's Olympic Peninsula, where it grows in open, wet meadows and the damp margins of coniferous forest, producing nodding white flowers with a yellow throat in spring above mottled leaves. Unlike many of its drought-tolerant relatives, it prefers consistently moist, humus-rich soil through spring and should be planted under light conifer or deciduous shade near a seep, pond margin, or woodland bed that does not dry out. It is best obtained as nursery-propagated bulbs or seed from a native-plant specialist given its very limited wild distribution, and once established it is best left undisturbed to slowly form a small colony.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil under deciduous shade, mimicking the cool forests of the Caucasus and northern Iran.

directions: Native to beech and mixed deciduous forests of the Caucasus region and northern Iran, Erythronium caucasicum is one of only a handful of Old World fawn lily species and produces a single nodding, creamy white to pale yellow flower above mottled, lance-shaped leaves in early spring. Grow it exactly as its better-known American cousins: in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil under deciduous trees that provide spring sun and summer shade, with a dry dormant period once the foliage withers. It is still uncommon in Western cultivation outside specialty alpine and bulb societies, so expect to source it from a woodland bulb specialist rather than a general garden center.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil under deciduous shade; among the most cold-hardy Erythronium species, tolerating harsh continental winters.

directions: Native to mountain forests and subalpine meadows of Siberia, Kazakhstan, and northwestern China, the Siberian fawn lily is extremely cold-hardy and one of the earliest Erythronium species to bloom, producing one or two nodding, lilac-pink to rose-purple flowers with a contrasting yellow or orange base above mottled green leaves. Plant bulbs in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil under deciduous shade where they receive bright spring light before the tree canopy closes in, then dry summer dormancy. It naturalizes well in a cold-climate woodland garden where many fawn lily species struggle, making it a good choice for colder regions of the upper Midwest or Mountain West.

planting.note: Plant divisions into gritty, humus-rich soil tucked into cool, shaded limestone or calcareous rock crevices with constant seepage moisture; avoid dry, hot sites.

directions: Sullivantia hapemanii is a disjunct relict species found clinging to cool, moist, calcareous cliff faces in a few isolated ranges of Wyoming and Montana, a pattern botanists attribute to its retreat into favorable microhabitats following Pleistocene glaciation. It forms a low rosette of rounded, scalloped leaves and sends up slender stalks of tiny white flowers in summer, thriving only where seep water keeps the rock face constantly damp. In cultivation it demands a shaded rock garden crevice or tufa wall with calcareous grit and permanent moisture at the roots, conditions that are difficult to replicate but reward specialists with a plant found almost nowhere else in gardens. Propagation is by division, since seed is rarely available commercially.
sources: Montana Field Guide (Montana Natural Heritage Program)

planting.note: Plant divisions into cool, constantly moist rock crevices or mossy ledges in deep shade near waterfalls or stream spray zones.

directions: Found clinging to wet basalt cliffs and spray-zone rock faces in the Columbia River Gorge and nearby Pacific Northwest canyons, Sullivantia oregana forms a small rosette of rounded, toothed leaves and slender racemes of tiny white flowers in summer, surviving only where mist or seepage keeps the rock constantly damp. In cultivation it needs a shaded rock garden or crevice planting with perpetual moisture, such as beside a man-made waterfall or seep wall, since it has no tolerance for drying out even briefly. It is a specialist's plant for a native rock garden rather than a general perennial border, propagated almost exclusively by division of existing clumps.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall just as the first rains arrive, in well-drained, humus-rich soil under light oak or chaparral shade; keep dry through the summer dormant season typical of California's Mediterranean climate.

directions: Foothill jepsonia is an unusual California endemic in the saxifrage family that breaks its own rules by flowering in fall rather than spring, sending up small pink, star-shaped blooms directly from a cormlike base before its rounded, toothed leaves even appear. It grows naturally on shaded banks and rocky slopes in oak woodland and chaparral margins, going completely dormant and leafless through the dry California summer. In the garden, plant corms in a lightly shaded, well-drained bed that receives winter and spring moisture but stays dry in summer, replicating its native Mediterranean-climate rhythm. It is a curiosity for native-plant and bulb specialists more than a mainstream ornamental.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall ahead of seasonal rains in well-drained soil under light shade on a slope or bank; keep dry and dormant through the summer.

directions: Parry's jepsonia grows on shaded, often north-facing slopes and rocky banks from southern California into Baja California Norte, blooming with small white to pale pink flowers on leafless stalks in autumn ahead of the rainy season, with rounded leaves following afterward. Like its close relative Jepsonia heterandra, it needs a Mediterranean-climate rhythm of winter-spring moisture and complete summer drought, making it best suited to a dry-shade native garden or rock garden bank in mild-winter regions. Plant corms shallowly in fast-draining, somewhat gravelly soil, and resist the urge to water during its leafless summer dormancy, when the corm is resting underground.

planting.note: Plant bulblets in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in a partly shaded rock garden or bank; foliage emerges with winter rain and dies back by early summer.

directions: Bolander's woodland star is a slender, bulb-forming perennial of rocky slopes and open woodland in the mountains of California and the Great Basin, producing a loose spray of small, deeply cleft white to pink star-shaped flowers on wiry stems above a basal rosette of lobed leaves in spring. Like other Lithophragma species it has a tight coevolved relationship with Greya moths, which both pollinate the flowers and lay eggs in the developing seed capsules. Grow it in a partly shaded rock garden or on a well-drained slope with lean, gritty soil, giving it moisture through its brief spring growth and allowing it to dry out and go dormant by early summer as it would in its native habitat.

planting.note: Plant small bulblets in fall in lean, well-drained soil on a partly shaded slope or rock garden; the plant goes fully dormant underground by midsummer.

directions: One of the most widespread woodland stars, Lithophragma glabrum ranges across rocky slopes, sagebrush steppe, and open montane woodland from British Columbia to California and east into the Rocky Mountains, producing clusters of small pink to white, star-shaped flowers on slender stems in early spring. Its tiny underground bulblets allow it to persist through dry summers and cold winters alike, re-sprouting each year with the return of cool, moist conditions. In the garden, plant in a partly shaded rock garden, gravel bed, or open woodland edge with sharp drainage, watering through the brief spring growing season and leaving the bed dry and undisturbed once the foliage withers in summer.

planting.note: Plant bulblets in fall in well-drained soil on a partly shaded grassy or rocky slope; grows through winter-spring rains and goes dormant by early summer.

directions: The San Francisco woodland star grows on grassy and rocky slopes and open woodland edges throughout the California Coast Ranges, where in early spring it produces airy clusters of pale pink to white flowers with deeply fringed, star-shaped petals above a rosette of lobed, hairy leaves. It depends on the region's Mediterranean rainfall pattern, growing actively through the cool, wet winter and spring before dying back completely for a dry summer dormancy. In a garden setting, give it a partly shaded, well-drained bank or rock garden with California-native bunchgrasses and other spring ephemerals, and avoid summer irrigation once the foliage has senesced.

planting.note: Plant bulblets in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in a partly shaded rock garden or slope; small and best grown close to a path edge where it can be appreciated.

directions: The mission woodland star is one of the smaller species in its genus, found on rocky outcrops and grassy slopes of the California Coast Ranges, producing tiny clusters of pale pink or white, deeply cut star-shaped flowers held just above a low rosette of rounded, lobed leaves in early spring. Its diminutive scale makes it best suited to a rock garden trough or the edge of a path where its delicate blooms can be seen up close rather than lost in a larger bed. Grow in lean, well-drained soil in light shade, with moisture during its brief winter-spring growth period and a dry summer rest, consistent with the Mediterranean climate of its native range.

planting.note: Plant bulblets in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in a lightly shaded rock garden mimicking high-elevation serpentine or rocky slopes.

directions: Restricted to the Siskiyou Mountains and nearby ranges of northern California and southern Oregon, this woodland star grows on rocky, often serpentine slopes at middle to high elevation, producing bell-shaped, pale pink to white flowers with a more cupped, less deeply fringed form than many of its relatives. In cultivation it wants the same lean, sharply drained, gritty soil of its native rock outcrops, sited in a partly shaded rock garden or alpine bed with moisture through its spring growing season and a dry, undisturbed dormancy over summer and winter. It is a good companion for other high-elevation Pacific Northwest rock garden natives such as Lewisia and dwarf Penstemon.

planting.note: Plant divisions into gritty, moist but well-drained soil tucked among rocks in partial shade, mimicking its native mountain cliff and talus habitat.

directions: Conimitella williamsii is the sole species in its genus, a saxifrage-family relict of rocky slopes, cliffs, and talus in the northern Rocky Mountains of Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, and Alberta, and has at various times been classified under Heuchera, Lithophragma, and Tellima before being given its own genus. It forms a basal rosette of rounded, scalloped leaves and sends up a slender stalk of small, bell-shaped white flowers in early summer. Grow it in a partly shaded rock garden or scree bed with gritty, humus-enriched soil that drains quickly but does not fully dry out, replicating the cool mountain rock habitat it depends on in the wild. Division of established clumps is the most reliable way to propagate it, since seed is rarely available commercially.
sources: Montana Field Guide (Montana Natural Heritage Program)

planting.note: Plant divisions into gritty, sharply drained soil wedged between rocks in partial shade, replicating its native high-elevation cliff and talus habitat; resents heavy, wet soil.

directions: Also long known as Boykinia jamesii, Telesonix jamesii is a high-elevation rock-crevice perennial of the Rocky Mountains, found from Alberta south through Montana, Wyoming, and Colorado into Utah and New Mexico, typically rooted into cracks in granite or limestone cliffs. It forms a low mat of rounded, toothed, somewhat leathery leaves and produces clusters of small, deep magenta-pink, cup-shaped flowers on short stalks in early summer, a striking color for an alpine saxifrage relative. In the garden it belongs in a scree bed, tufa wall, or crevice garden with very sharp drainage and light shade from the hottest afternoon sun, since in nature it roots into mineral crevices with little organic matter. Division of offsets is the usual propagation method, as it resents root disturbance and transplants best while small.
